les: Wat klei, gras en riet kan word
kaps_punt: in Afrika het mense vir honderde jare materiale verwerk, soos: kleipotte en bakstene, mandjies, hoede, matte, grasdakke gemaak van plantmateriaal soos grasse en riete

items.bewering: In Afrika verwerk mense al honderde jare lank materiale met hulle hande.
items.blok: Werk wat al honderde jare aanhou
items.bron: Wikipedia 'African pottery' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_pottery): pottery developed across the southern Sahara and Sahel in the tenth millennium BP; Wikipedia 'Lydenburg heads' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydenburg_heads): terracotta from Mpumalanga c. AD 500. True as stated (at least hundreds). It understates the age, since it is thousands of years for pottery, but it is not false and it follows the CAPS wording. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Hulle gebruik hulle vingers, 'n mes en 'n skerp naald as gereedskap.
items.blok: Werk wat al honderde jare aanhou
items.bron: Britannica, 'Sewed coiling' (https://www.britannica.com/art/sewed-coiling), search extract: coils are sewn 'using a needle or an awl'. Western Australian Museum, 'Coil stitch' (https://museum.wa.gov.au/explore/intertwined/stitch-types/coil-stitch): wrapping is threaded 'using a needle'. Homo Faber / Michelangelo Foundation, 'Zulu Cone Baskets' (https://2022.homofaber.com/en/ecollection/zulu-cone-basket-qukqf): ilala leaves are 'cut into fine strips'. Zulu weavers most often use an awl, described as a 'needle-like tool' (The Ethnic Home). Britannica accepts either tool, so 'skerp naald' holds. The sentence lists tools and does not claim these are the only ones. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: 'n Gladde ronde klippie vryf die buitekant van 'n kleipot glad.
items.blok: Werk wat al honderde jare aanhou
items.bron: 'Zulu pottery technology and group identity in the Phongolo Basin, South Africa' (research article, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/292775282), abstract/search extract: Zulu potters rub a pebble over the vessel surface until it is polished. ResearchGate figure 'A potter burnishing the base of a steaming pot using a pebble' (https://www.researchgate.net/figure/A-potter-burnishing-the-base-of-a-steaming-pot-using-a-pebble_fig6_257506052). Strauss & Co lot description of Nesta Nala's work: 'A burnished fired clay ukhamba' (https://www.straussart.co.za/auctions/lot/13-jun-2022/73). Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Mense maak vandag nog kleipotte, en vandag nog mandjies uit gras.
items.blok: Werk wat al honderde jare aanhou
items.bron: Metropolitan Museum of Art: an ukhamba by Siphiwe Nellie MaS'Khakhane Nala, a living potter of the Nala family (https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/909740). Ilala Weavers, KwaZulu-Natal, a working basket enterprise (https://www.ilala.co.za/the-baskets/). Homo Faber, Zulu cone baskets by the current Ilala Weavers community. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Nat klei is sag en jy vorm dit met die hand tot 'n pot.
items.bron: Timothy S. Y. Lam Museum of Anthropology, Wake Forest University, 'Zulu Beer Pot' (https://lammuseum.wfu.edu/2023/04/zulu-beer-pot/): 'constructed with terracotta coils wrapped around a flat base, which are smoothed to create very thin walls', which is hand-built. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Die pot droog eers stadig uit.
items.bron: Digitalfire, 'Drying ceramics without cracks' (https://digitalfire.com/article/drying+ceramics+without+cracks), and pottery drying guidance (search extracts): greenware must dry slowly and evenly, because uneven shrinkage cracks it. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Die droë pot gaan dan in 'n vuur en word hard gebak.
items.bron: Strauss & Co, 'Pit-fired earthenware pot with relief patterns by Nesta Nala' (https://www.straussart.co.za/auctions/lot/316-26-jun-2024/52). Lam Museum 'Zulu Beer Pot': 'The pots are fired twice'. Traditional Zulu pots are fired in an open fire pit. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Ongebakte klei word in water weer sag, maar gebakte klei bly hard.
items.bron: The Pottery Wheel, 'What happens to clay when it is fired' (https://thepotterywheel.com/what-happens-to-clay-when-it-is-fired/): unfired clay 'slakes down' in water; after dehydroxylation (complete around 600 °C) the change is irreversible, and wet bisque 'stays intact'. Also RSC Education, 'The chemistry of pottery' (https://edu.rsc.org/feature/the-chemistry-of-pottery/2020245.article). Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Die klei het ander eienskappe gekry en die pot is nou verwerkte materiaal.
items.bron: Victorian Department of Education, 'Properties of natural and processed materials' (https://www.education.vic.gov.au/school/teachers/teachingresources/discipline/science/continuum/Pages/naturalproc.aspx): processed materials are 'modified from natural materials ... to fulfil a particular purpose'. Firing turns clay into ceramic, an irreversible change (see the previous item). Strictly, the pot is an object made of processed material (fired clay), but CAPS itself lists clay pots as examples, so this is not an error. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Bakstene begin ook by nat klei.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Mudbrick' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudbrick): 'a mixture of mud (containing loam, clay, sand, and water)'. Wikipedia 'Adobe' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adobe): 'earth mixed with water'. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Sand en strooi of gras word eers bygemeng.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Adobe' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adobe): 'straw or grass is OFTEN added to help the bricks shrink more uniformly as they dry'. Wikipedia 'Mudbrick' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudbrick): mud 'from some locations required sand, chopped straw, or other binders'. So even for sun-dried bricks this is not a fixed step. In the lesson the sentence comes before the split into fired and sun-dried bricks, so it also claims straw or grass goes into fired bricks. None of the sources describes that as usual practice. Organic additives in fired bricks appear in the literature as special pore-forming additives, not as the normal method.
items.regstelling: Narrow the quantifier. Do not cut the sentence. Say that sand and straw or grass is often, or for many bricks, mixed in first, and not that it happens to every brick. Better still, tie the straw or grass to the sun-dried bricks, where the sources place it. Keep the next sentence (the brick cracks much less easily when it dries), because it is correct. Make sure the order of the sentences no longer implies that fired bricks also contain straw or grass.

items.bewering: Die steen kraak dan baie minder maklik wanneer hy droog word.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Adobe': straw binds the brick and lets it dry evenly, 'thereby preventing cracking due to uneven shrinkage rates through the brick'. Experimental study, Construction and Building Materials (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0950061817304385), search extract: straw 'minimizes shrinkage and prevents occurring cracks'. The claim holds only once the preceding item is fixed, because it depends on it. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Party bakstene word ook in 'n vuur hard gebak. Ander bakstene word net in die son droog gemaak en glad nie gebak nie.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Brick clamp' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick_clamp): unbaked bricks stacked with fuel and fired. Search extracts include a Malawi clamp and brick making in Vhembe, South Africa (MDPI Sustainability 13(19):10659), where bricks are sun-dried and then fired. Wikipedia 'Adobe': 'unfired masonry units', sun-dried. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Mense sny gras en riet en maak die halms eers in die son droog.
items.bron: Florida Museum, Seminole baskets technique (https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/sflarch/ethnographic-collections/seminole-baskets/technique/): 'the grass is washed in water, bundled, and placed in the sun to dry'. Homo Faber, Zulu cone baskets: ilala 'first harvested and dried'. Search extract on Zulu icansi: incema is 'sun-dried in the open air' before weaving. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Groen halms krimp later in die mandjie.
items.bron: Basketry practice sources (search extracts, consistent across independent craft sources, e.g. Joybilee Farm https://joybileefarm.com/craft-rustic-willow-basket-choosing-materials/ and grass-weaving guides): fresh material shrinks as it dries and leaves a loose weave, so material is dried first so that it shrinks before weaving. These are craft sources, not museum sources, but they agree and the physics (water loss means shrinkage) is uncontroversial. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Droë halms breek maklik, daarom maak baie wewers hulle weer klam.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Basket weaving' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basket_weaving): dried material is 'soaked or boiled to increase pliability'. Basketry sources: dried material is brittle and is soaked or sprayed to restore flexibility. For a southern African grass: mosea grass for the Basotho hat is 'placed in water to soften' (Steemit, a weak source). On how absolute the claim is: 'maklik' is a tendency, and the second half is already correctly quantified ('baie wewers'). The same weak source calls mosea 'flexible even when dry', and incema mats are woven from dry rushes. Neither case contradicts the sentence, because it does not say every weaver dampens every stalk. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: So verander mense die halms self.
items.bron: Follows from the two previous items: drying shrinks the stalk permanently, and dampening makes it pliable again. Note for the person reading: dampening is a temporary change, so together with the 'verwerkte materiaal' entry it makes a dampened stalk count as processed material (see that item). REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Party halms word gevleg of geweef, maar baie mandjies en hoede word gerol.
items.bron: Coiling as the hallmark of Zulu basketry: Missouri State University Art History exhibition (https://blogs.missouristate.edu/arthistory/african-basketry-researched-by-lindsay-werner-caitlin-baker-and-randi-ryder-2/). Hats: Powerhouse Museum, mokorotlo (https://collection.powerhouse.com.au/object/380042): 'constructed by coiling bunches of reeds that are held in place by rows of twining', with 'bands of plaited reeds' on the brim. Plaiting and weaving are also used (Wikipedia 'Basket weaving'). REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: 'n Bondel halms word tot 'n tou gedraai en met repies palmblaar vasgesteek.
items.bron: Britannica 'Sewed coiling' (https://www.britannica.com/art/sewed-coiling), search extract: the foundation is a bundle coiled upward, and each coil is 'pierced and bound to the preceding one'. Western Australian Museum 'Coil stitch': grasses 'are bundled together and then wrapped with stitching ... through the previous coil'. Ilala Weavers (search extract): grasses 'formed into tight coils around which the Ilala palm fronds are wrapped to form the cord'. The Ethnic Home: the palm strips are stitched 'around the coil'. None of the sources describes the bundle being twisted into a rope. The rope-like cord comes from the palm strip wound tightly round a straight bundle, and the strip is also what joins each round to the round below. 'Tot 'n tou gedraai' teaches twisting, which is the wrong mechanism, and it leaves out the part that makes the basket hold together. Also: in the mokorotlo hat the coils are held by rows of twining, not by palm leaf (Powerhouse), so the sentence cannot describe 'mandjies en hoede' together.
items.regstelling: Describe coiling as it works: the stalks stay a bundle and are not twisted. A thin strip of palm leaf is wound tightly round the bundle and stitched to the round below, while the bundle is laid round and round in a spiral. The wrapped bundle can still be pictured as a rope, as long as twisting is not given as the method. Tie the palm-leaf sentence to baskets, not to hats.

items.bewering: Vir 'n mat bind gare die halms langs mekaar vas.
items.bron: Phansi Museum, Durban, via Google Arts & Culture, 'Ucansi / Reed Mat' (https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/ucansi-reed-mat/8gFpwZpHCmHe8g): 'made from incema (juncus kraussii) by tying the rushes closely together with twine'. Note: incema is a rush, not a grass or reed in the strict sense, but the sentence does not name incema, and grass mats also exist. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Hierdie werk verander nie waarvan 'n halm gemaak is nie.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Weaving' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weaving): interlacing threads at right angles. Coiling and binding are likewise purely physical placement and stitching (Britannica, WA Museum). Nothing in the process changes the substance of the stalk. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Maar 'n mat of mandjie kry eienskappe wat los halms nie het nie. Dit hou as een stuk bymekaar en is sterker as enige halm.
items.bron: 'Advances in Textile Structural Composites', PMC (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9959984/), search extract: interlacing 'produces a coherent and stable structure', and 'the threads take the load together'. Zulu coiling described as 'a tight, interlocking structure that is strong yet flexible' (Missouri State exhibition). 'Sterker as enige halm' holds, because the load is shared across many stalks. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Vir 'n dak sny mense party grasse wat al droog staan.
items.bron: Thatchers' Association of South Africa, reproducing SANS 10407:2004 and 'A Guide to Good Thatching Practice' (http://waterfrontthatchers.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/TASA_-_Article_-_Specification_for_Grass.pdf): grass must 'not be cut in the growing season' and must be 'fully grown and matured'; it is 'usually cut from mid-winter to August, after growth has stopped and the first hard frost has killed the leaves'. 'Party grasse' is correctly narrowed. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Die hele dak lê skuins en die droë halms lê almal skuins na onder.
items.bron: Building Conservation, 'Thatched Roofs: An Introduction' (https://www.buildingconservation.com/articles/thatchrf/thatchrf.htm): steep pitches shed water fast. Hendricks Architecture (https://www.hendricksarchitect.com/architecture/thatch-roofing-in-rain-and-snow), search extract: pitch no less than 45 degrees. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Die reën loop dan van halm na halm en drup by die rand af.
items.bron: Building Conservation, 'Thatched Roofs: An Introduction': 'Water is transferred down the roof from stem to stem until it drops from the eave.' REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Die halms lê in dik lae op mekaar.
items.bron: SANS 10407:2004, Table 1 (via the TASA document above): thatch layer 175 mm for common thatching grass and 200 mm for coarse grass. The Thatcher's Art FAQ (https://www.thatchco.com/thatchpg/faq.htm): layers about 12 inches thick. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Meestal word net die buitenste halms nat.
items.bron: The Thatcher's Art FAQ (https://www.thatchco.com/thatchpg/faq.htm): 'Moisture typically does not absorb into the thatch bundles more than 1 or 2 inches.' Hendricks Architecture, search extract: at the correct angle water does not penetrate 'more than an inch (25mm) or so'. 'Meestal' matches the sources' 'typically'. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Die dik laag hou daardie nat buitekant ver van die binnekant af. So kry die hele laag 'n eienskap wat los halms nie het nie.
items.bron: Follows from the two previous items: about 25–50 mm of wetting against a 175–200 mm layer (SANS 10407; Thatcher's Art FAQ). The Thatcher's Art FAQ: bundled stems together form an 'impenetrable shell of waterproofing' that single stems do not. The block attributes the roof's water-shedding to slope plus thickness, which is correct. REWRITTEN BLOCK. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Mense kies meestal die materiaal vir wat sy eienskappe kan doen.
items.bron: Examples of selection by property: ilala palm is chosen for its 'natural waxy coating' that makes watertight baskets possible (Baskets of Africa, https://basketsofafrica.com/weaving-zulu-ilala-palm-baskets-in-south-africa/); incema is chosen because it is 'strong, durable, and yet easy to bend' (search extract on icansi); SANS 10407 requires thatching material 'of a type that has a history of successful use in a locality'. 'Meestal' keeps it a tendency. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Klei is sag genoeg om te vorm en dit word hard in die vuur.
items.bron: As for the pot items above: Lam Museum (hand coiling of wet clay); The Pottery Wheel and RSC Education (firing makes clay hard, irreversibly). Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Gras en riet is lank en sterk, en klam halms buig sonder om te breek.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Phragmites australis' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phragmites_australis): culms 1.5–4 m tall. Soaking restores pliability (Wikipedia 'Basket weaving'; basketry sources). This is a general tendency: a damp stalk still breaks if bent too sharply, but read as a generic statement it matches what the sources say pliability is. Note: for a mat, the stalks are bound side by side and not bent, so 'bend without breaking' mainly serves baskets and hats. That is not false. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: Die eienskap kom eerste en die gebruik volg daaruit.
items.bron: Not a historical 'first'. It restates the selection principle confirmed above (ilala, incema, thatching grass chosen for properties). It is a design principle and not a date claim, so it is not at superlative risk. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: verwerkte materiaal: Materiaal wat mense verander het sodat dit ander eienskappe kry.
items.bron: Victorian Department of Education, 'Properties of natural and processed materials': processed materials are 'modified from natural materials ... designed and manufactured to fulfil a particular purpose', on a continuum from wood to plywood to MDF to paper. Materials-processing definitions (search extract, Britannica): processing shapes material and 'improves its properties'. The entry is accurate. REWRITTEN ENTRY, read with the rest of the lesson removed, as asked. (1) The fired pot fits cleanly: people changed the clay, and it gained hardness that does not return to soft in water. (2) The mat fits only if 'materiaal' is read as the woven whole: the stalks are changed only by drying and dampening, and the new properties (holds as one piece, stronger) belong to the mat, not to the stalk. That is the loose end of the Victorian continuum, but it is within it. (3) What else it fits: paper, glass, steel and plastic, which are correct. It also fits cooked food and a sun-dried brick, which are defensible. And it fits a DAMPENED stalk and WET clay: people changed them so that they bend or become soft. Those are temporary changes that the lesson itself treats as preparation, and the pot paragraph makes permanence the test ('gebakte klei bly hard'), while the definition has no such test. That is a scope decision, not a false fact, so it is not marked contradicted. A person should decide whether the definition needs a permanence criterion.

items.bewering: halm: Die lang dun stingel van 'n grasplant of van riet.
items.bron: Van Dale, Groot woordenboek der Nederlandse taal, via ensie.nl (https://www.ensie.nl/van-dale/halm), the Dutch cognate: 'gras- of graanstengel'. Wikipedia 'Phragmites australis': reed stems are called 'culms', the botanical term for grass stems. Reed is itself a grass (Poaceae), so 'of van riet' is correct. No Afrikaans dictionary entry was reached online, and this rests on the Dutch cognate. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: riet: 'n Hoë grasagtige plant met lang dun stingels wat mense verwerk.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Phragmites australis': 'a species of flowering plant in the grass family Poaceae'; stems 1.5–4 m, 5–10 mm broad; 'the primary source of thatch'. 'Grasagtig' understates this, because reed is a grass, but it is not false. Read alone, it also fits papyrus and other sedges, which are commonly called reed anyway. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: vleg: Om drie of meer halms om die beurt oor mekaar te vou.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Braid' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braid): 'formed by interlacing three or more strands', the simplest being three strands. The count and the alternation are correct. For the language check, not a factual finding: in a plait strands are crossed or laid over each other, not folded ('vou'), and a learner handling a dry stalk who folds it will break it. Checked in full this round.

items.bewering: weef: Om halms bo-oor en onderdeur ander halms te laat loop.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Weaving': 'two distinct sets of yarns or threads are interlaced at right angles'. Over-and-under is the interlacing. Read alone, it also describes a plait, which also runs over and under, so the two entries do not separate the techniques cleanly. That is not false. Checked in full this round.

opsomming: Twee meganisme-bewerings is te wyd en moet reggemaak word: die baksteensin laat sand en strooi of gras in álle bakstene gaan, ook gebakte, terwyl bronne sê dit word 'dikwels' bygevoeg, veral by songedroogde stene; en die rolwerksin sê 'n bondel halms word tot 'n tou gedraai, terwyl bronne 'n reguit bondel beskryf wat met 'n palmblaarrepie toegedraai en aan die ry daaronder vasgesteek word. Die herskrewe bewerings oor droog word, weer klam maak, die sterkte van gevlegte werk en die grasdak hou almal stand, en die begrip 'verwerkte materiaal' is korrek, maar pas alleen gelees ook op 'n klam gemaakte halm en nat klei, omdat dit geen toets vir 'n blywende verandering het nie; 'n mens moet besluit of dit genoeg is.
